title: Korea Opens First Humanoid Robot Data Factory in Daejeon
summary: KIMM's AI Humanoid Data Factory uses 12 bipedal robots and human teleoperation to produce training data for general-purpose autonomous machines.
body_markdown:
#### 💡 TL;DR


- KIMM opened South Korea's first dedicated humanoid robot training data factory on November 3, 2026, using 12 bipedal robots.
- Human operators remotely control robots to demonstrate physical tasks, generating datasets for AI models to learn manipulation and movement.
- The facility supports Korea's K-Moonshot AI Humanoid Mission and will gradually open to external researchers by late 2027.


South Korea has established the country's first dedicated facility for producing training data for humanoid robots, addressing one of the most persistent challenges in developing general-purpose autonomous machines. The Korea Institute of Machinery and Materials (KIMM) in Daejeon officially launched the AI Humanoid Data Factory on November 3, 2026, in collaboration with the Electronics and Telecommunications Research Institute (ETRI). The facility uses 12 bipedal robots operated remotely by humans to generate datasets that teach AI models how to perform physical tasks.


## Release Date and Facility Details


Officially launched on November 3, 2026, the Data Factory represents a significant investment in physical AI infrastructure. The facility was developed by KIMM's Global TOP Strategic Research Group for Self-Growing AI Humanoids under Dr Chan Hun Park, with support from the Ministry of Science and ICT. It forms part of South Korea's broader K-Moonshot AI Humanoid Mission, which aims to strengthen domestic humanoid technologies and reduce dependence on capabilities developed overseas. The facility is scheduled to open gradually to external researchers and industry partners by late 2027.


## How Teleoperation Generates Training Data


The factory uses teleoperation, a process where human operators remotely control robots while their movements and interactions are recorded. These demonstrations provide examples from which artificial intelligence models can learn how physical tasks are performed. During the opening ceremony, humanoid robots demonstrated retrieving items from refrigerators, handling laundry, arranging furniture, and operating vehicle controls. The Korean-developed KAIROS robot performed precise object manipulation and full-body motion imitation.


Conventional industrial robots execute programmed movements in predictable conditions, making them effective for repetitive tasks. General-purpose humanoids must respond to instructions and handle varied situations, requiring systems that connect visual information, language, movement, and physical object properties. Each task demonstration produces data showing how robots should position themselves, establish grips, apply force, and maintain balance during operations.


## Training Workflow and Model Development


Once operators guide humanoid robots through activities involving arms, legs, and full-body movements, the resulting information trains models intended to interpret instructions, recognize surroundings, and generate appropriate movements without continuous human intervention. After training, AI models are deployed onto physical robots for testing, with their subsequent performance producing additional data incorporated into later training cycles. Researchers use this feedback to refine models, identify weaknesses, and assess whether improved capabilities can be reproduced across different tasks and robotic platforms.


The programme also supports the K-Humanoid standard platform, with researchers working toward AI models that can be adapted to different robots rather than restricted to a single machine design. This transferability could eventually reduce task-specific training requirements when introducing new robotic hardware, although differences between machines remain a substantial engineering consideration.


## International Context and Competing Approaches


Korea's facility joins international efforts to develop humanoid robotics training infrastructure. NVIDIA's Isaac GR00T platform combines physical robot demonstrations, simulated movements, and other training sources to develop foundation models for humanoid reasoning and movement. Google DeepMind's Gemini Robotics 2.5 models, introduced in November 2026, extend work on vision-language-action systems capable of interpreting instructions and generating physical movements across different robotic configurations.


These organizations pursue different approaches but share a demanding requirement: training models on information that adequately represents the physical situations robots will encounter. Large quantities of demonstration data can improve learning opportunities, yet the diversity and relevance of those demonstrations remain critical. A robot trained repeatedly on narrow selections of successful operations may perform well in familiar conditions while struggling with objects or situations outside its training experience.


## Industrial Applications and Practical Challenges


Many industrial activities still depend on equipment designed around human movements, from vehicle controls and machinery interfaces to inspection stations and maintenance procedures. Humanoid robots capable of manipulating these existing systems could eventually undertake selected operations without requiring every workstation to be redesigned around conventional automation equipment. The vehicle control demonstrations at KIMM provide early examples of the physical interactions involved.


However, real-world deployment faces substantial obstacles. Construction sites present uneven surfaces, weather exposure, changing layouts, and the movement of workers and heavy machinery. Even relatively routine activities change significantly between locations. A component easy to handle on a clean workbench may be awkward to manipulate when surrounded by other materials or positioned inside an incomplete structure. Safety would require extensive evaluation before humanoid robots could routinely work alongside construction personnel or operate equipment under load.


## What This Means


Korea's dedicated humanoid data production facility provides researchers with direct access to the machines generating training information and the opportunity to refine demonstrations through repeated testing. Its domestic focus reflects the strategic value increasingly attached to AI training resources, particularly where those resources depend on specialized hardware and physical experimentation. For industries exploring how humanoid robots might eventually fit into their operations, the project offers insight into the considerable training infrastructure required before machines can move beyond controlled demonstrations and undertake dependable work. The facility's initial fleet of 12 robots represents a starting point for accumulating the datasets needed to develop more capable autonomous systems, with practical applications likely emerging first in controlled industrial environments before expanding to more demanding operational contexts.
